title: My son Absalom (2 Samuel 18:33)
hookLine: the rebellious son dies and David wishes he had died instead
carry: would god I had died for thee
last: I HAVE SINNED AGAINST THE LORD.

cards: Nathan warned David that trouble would rise from inside his own house, and it does. Years of it. A terrible wrong between his children, a revenge killing, a son sent into exile, then brought home but kept at arm's length.

That son is Absalom, handsome and well-known for his thick hair. He sits by the city gate, listens to people's complaints, and tells them: if only I were judge, you'd get justice. Slowly he wins the hearts of Israel.
Then he declares himself king, and David has to flee Jerusalem on foot, weeping as he climbs the Mount of Olives. Father and son are now at war.

teach.b: The armies meet in a forest. Before the battle, David gives his commanders one order, in front of everyone, and the Douay-Rheims puts it tenderly: "Save me the boy Absalom." The boy.
A grown man leading a rebellion to take his father's throne, and David still calls him the boy.
The battle goes against Absalom. Riding a mule under a great oak, his head catches in the branches, the mule runs on, and he's left hanging between heaven and earth.
David's commander Joab finds him and, against the king's order, kills him. Messengers run to David, who is waiting between the city gates. The first is vague.
The second says it plainly: may all the king's enemies be as that young man is. And David breaks.

He climbs to the room above the gate, weeping: my son Absalom, Absalom my son, and in the Douay-Rheims: "would to God that I might die for thee." Older English Bibles put it as would God I had died for thee.
Count how many times he says my son. He has won the war and lost his child, and he would rather have died himself.

teach.h: A FATHER WHO'D DIE IN HIS PLACE.
teach.b: Some Christian readers hear something more in that cry: a father who would die in place of a rebellious son.

teach.h: WOULD GOD I HAD DIED FOR THEE.
teach.b: David could only wish it. For them, in Christ, God did it. And that's week fifty-eight: a shepherd chosen, a giant, a friend, a cave, a dance, a confession, and a father's grief.

how: Catholics hear Absalom's rebellion and David's grief in the weekday Mass readings, and Catholics pray for divided families at Mass and in the rosary, some asking the intercession of Saint Monica, honored as a patron of parents with wayward children.

it says his head stuck in the oak. his heavy hair comes earlier in the story, so some readers connect the two.
David ordered his men to spare Absalom
"save me the boy Absalom," in the hearing of all the people.
David celebrated when he heard the battle was won
he asked first about his son, then went up and wept: my son, my son.

games.q: you're King David. your son has tried to take your throne and drove you from Jerusalem. your army is about to fight his. what do you tell your commanders?
games.why: David orders them, in front of everyone, to spare his son. Joab kills him anyway, and the victory turns into grief.

practice: Bring to mind a family that's split, maybe yours: a parent and child who don't speak, siblings who stopped sharing a table. Don't try to solve it; just hold them, the way David held Absalom's name in the middle of a war.
If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, simply wish them peace.

wordCard.voice: Absalom. The rebel son David still called the boy, and cried over, wishing he had died in his place. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: my son. David repeats it again and again in his lament over Absalom.

carryVoice: Your line: would god I had died for thee. Even in a war, he still called him the boy. Rest well; a new week starts tomorrow.
